title: How to Size GPUs for AI Inference and TCO Without Overspending | NVIDIA Technical Blog
gist: NVIDIA lays out a GPU inference sizing framework built on four use-case token profiles (chatbots, agents, content generation, translation), a core-and-flex capex/opex capacity split, and three memory-footprint levers — quantization, pruning, distillation. Concrete numbers include FP8 post-training quantization cutting Llama-3.1-8B weight memory 43.5% from 16.06GB to 9.08GB with no retraining, and a depth-pruned ~6B Qwen3-8B student running 30% faster than Qwen3-4B at higher MMLU (72.5 vs 70.0). The subtext is notable: the GPU vendor is actively teaching enterprises how to buy fewer and smaller GPUs.

themes.theme: Token profiles as the sizing primitive

insights.claim: Inference workloads map to four token-pattern archetypes with radically different infrastructure footprints: chatbots/copilots (2,000-8,000 input, 200-800 output), AI agents (>128,000 cached input, 500-1,000 input, 200-300 output), content generation (200-1,000 input, 1,000-4,000 output), and translation (200-1,000 in and out).
insights.speaker: Prerana Gambhir
insights.so_what: Forecasting datacenter GPU demand from user counts alone is wrong by orders of magnitude; the agent archetype's >128K cached-context profile is the single largest memory driver and the reason agentic adoption converts to disproportionate GPU capex.
insights.locator: Know your use case: Where sizing and TCO begin

insights.claim: Deep-research AI agents consume more than 128,000 cached input tokens while emitting only 200-300 output tokens, an extreme input-to-output asymmetry versus content generation which inverts it at up to 4,000 output tokens on 200-1,000 input.
insights.speaker: Prerana Gambhir
insights.so_what: Prefill-heavy agentic traffic and decode-heavy generation traffic stress different parts of the GPU, so the workload mix determines which hardware generation and memory-bandwidth profile a buyer actually needs.
insights.locator: Use CaseCached Input TokensInput TokensOutput Tokens

insights.claim: The published token figures are labeled illustrative, with the authors warning that values observed in real-world production could vary drastically from the table.
insights.speaker: Prerana Gambhir
insights.so_what: Treat the framework as structure, not as inputs to a model; anyone building GPU demand estimates on these figures inherits large error bars.
insights.quote: these are illustrative figures, the values observed in real-world production scenarios could vary drastically
insights.locator: Table 1. Use cases for GPU input and output tokens

themes.theme: The sizing input variables that actually bind

insights.claim: Concurrency, not daily active user count, is the binding constraint on GPU memory and latency, so headline user growth is a poor proxy for infrastructure need.
insights.speaker: Prerana Gambhir
insights.so_what: When evaluating AI application companies, ask for peak concurrency and burst profile rather than DAU growth — that is what sets the cost floor.
insights.quote: High concurrency strains GPU memory and latency more than raw DAUs.

insights.claim: Cache hit rate is a first-class sizing variable: input tokens served from the KV cache skip prefill entirely, cutting time-to-first-token and cost per request and lowering the GPU capacity needed to serve identical traffic.
insights.speaker: Prerana Gambhir
insights.so_what: Prompt-caching efficiency is an underappreciated margin lever for inference providers — two vendors on identical hardware can have materially different unit economics based on cache hit rate alone.
insights.quote: A higher cache hit rate skips prefill for those tokens, reducing TTFT and cost per request, which can lower the GPU capacity you need for the same traffic.

insights.claim: The authors argue larger models are not automatically better and point buyers toward mainstream or smaller fine-tuned models that fit their data and latency requirements.
insights.speaker: Prerana Gambhir
insights.so_what: A hardware vendor steering customers toward smaller models signals confidence that total token volume, not per-token compute, drives its demand curve — and it undercuts the thesis that frontier-scale models capture all enterprise inference.
insights.quote: Bigger isn’t always better.

insights.claim: Latency is not one number: TTFT average, 99th-percentile latency, and intertoken latency are separate targets, and picking which one matters is presented as a prerequisite sizing decision.
insights.speaker: Prerana Gambhir
insights.so_what: SLA definition drives hardware selection; vendors quoting only average TTFT are hiding the tail behavior that determines real provisioning cost.

insights.claim: Contract length should follow traffic predictability — stable predictable traffic justifies long-term contracts or on-prem infrastructure, while volatile or experimental workloads belong on flexible on-demand or spot capacity.
insights.speaker: Prerana Gambhir
insights.so_what: Explains the observed bifurcation between multi-year GPU commitments from mature AI products and spot-heavy consumption from experimental ones — a useful lens for reading neocloud backlog quality.
insights.quote: Stable, predictable traffic may warrant long-term contracts or on-prem infrastructure. Volatile or experimental workloads benefit from flexible, on-demand (cloud or spot) capacity.

insights.claim: The recommended capacity architecture is a 'core-and-flex' split: a baseline of on-prem or reserved cloud GPUs sized for steady-state traffic, layered with public-cloud spot or on-demand GPUs absorbing surges, launches, and experiments.
insights.speaker: Prerana Gambhir
insights.so_what: If enterprises adopt this, hyperscalers and neoclouds keep the volatile marginal demand while the predictable base migrates on-prem — implying steadier server OEM orders and lumpier cloud GPU revenue.
insights.quote: This model strikes a balance between capital efficiency (capex) and operational agility (opex), ensuring you aren’t overprovisioning or stifling growth.

insights.claim: The stated purpose of the core tier is insulation from GPU price volatility, framing owned or reserved capacity as a hedge instrument rather than just a cost choice.
insights.speaker: Prerana Gambhir
insights.so_what: Expectation of continued GPU spot-price volatility is being baked into enterprise architecture guidance — supportive of long-dated capacity contracts and of the reserved-instance pricing spread.
insights.quote: This reduces the risk of price volatility and ensures a reliable service for the bulk of your users.

insights.claim: Colocation becomes necessary specifically under rapid expansion or data-residency requirements, and is otherwise skippable for organizations with on-prem data and stable capacity.
insights.speaker: Prerana Gambhir
insights.so_what: Colo demand is driven by growth rate and regulation rather than baseline AI adoption — a narrower demand driver than the general AI buildout narrative implies.

insights.claim: Mis-sizing cuts both ways: overprovisioned capacity drops utilization and raises cost per token, while undersized capacity constrains throughput and latency, making right-sizing to the specific model and prompt lengths the mechanism that keeps performance and cost aligned.
insights.speaker: Prerana Gambhir
insights.so_what: Cost per token is a utilization metric as much as a hardware metric; low-utilization GPU fleets are a hidden margin drag worth probing in any AI infrastructure disclosure.
insights.quote: When capacity runs ahead of what a workload needs, utilization drops and cost per token rises; when it runs behind the workload’s memory or compute demands, throughput and latency are constrained.

themes.theme: Vertical sizing scenarios and memory tiers

insights.claim: A financial-services copilot handling 5,000 input and 500 output tokens per query needs roughly 24GB of GPU memory for a 7-8B model, scaling to 48GB for a 13B model to leave KV cache headroom, with sub-1-second TTFT and 10-50 concurrent sessions.
insights.speaker: Prerana Gambhir
insights.so_what: Mainstream enterprise copilots land in the 24-48GB memory tier, well below flagship datacenter parts — meaning much of enterprise inference demand is addressable by lower-ASP GPUs.
insights.locator: Financial services – Copilot for relationship managers

insights.claim: A drug-discovery AI agent processing 20,000 input and 2,000 output tokens requires GPU memory typically exceeding 80GB per unit, with 16K-32K long-context models and a sub-2-second TTFT target for 20-30 concurrent researchers.
insights.speaker: Prerana Gambhir
insights.so_what: Agentic long-context workloads are the segment that actually forces 80GB+ parts — the strongest demand signal for high-memory SKUs and HBM content per GPU.
insights.quote: Opt for very high memory capacity, typically exceeding 80GB per unit
insights.locator: Life sciences — AI agent for drug discovery

insights.claim: A marketing content generator running 3-7B models on 500-input/2,000-output requests fits in 16-24GB of GPU memory, and an enterprise translation platform can run on entry-level 8-16GB GPUs when orchestrated in a distributed cloud environment.
insights.speaker: Prerana Gambhir
insights.so_what: Two of four mainstream enterprise use cases fit on sub-24GB GPUs, which supports a large and price-competitive mid-range inference market rather than exclusive concentration in flagship accelerators.
insights.quote: Entry-level GPUs (8-16GB of memory) are suitable for handling requests, particularly when orchestrated in a distributed, scalable cloud environment.
insights.locator: Technology consulting — Large scale translation platform

insights.claim: Precision choice is dictated by domain risk rather than cost: compliance-critical financial and scientific workloads are steered to FP16/BF16 or higher, while translation and code work is deemed adequate at FP16 or INT8.
insights.speaker: Prerana Gambhir
insights.so_what: Regulated verticals will adopt low-precision inference more slowly, so the efficiency gains that lower GPU demand accrue unevenly across industries.
insights.locator: Precision: For knowledge-intensive and compliance-critical tasks

insights.claim: FP8 post-training quantization with NVIDIA Model Optimizer cut Llama-3.1-8B weight memory from 16.06GB to 9.08GB, a 43.5% reduction achieved with no retraining.
insights.speaker: Prerana Gambhir
insights.so_what: A ~44% memory cut for near-zero engineering effort is effectively a free capacity expansion across the installed base, which dampens incremental GPU demand per unit of served traffic.
insights.quote: FP8 quantization reduces Llama-3.1-8B weight memory from 16.06GB to 9.08GB — a 43.5% reduction with no retraining.

insights.claim: Reducing memory footprint is described as one of the highest-leverage TCO moves because it can let a workload drop an entire GPU tier, not merely trim utilization.
insights.speaker: Prerana Gambhir
insights.so_what: Tier-dropping is a step-function cost change, so optimization adoption can produce discrete downshifts in enterprise GPU mix rather than smooth reductions in volume.
insights.quote: A smaller footprint lets you serve on compact or lower-cost GPUs, and in many cases drop an entire GPU tier.
insights.locator: Optimizing models for a better TCO

insights.claim: FP8 is recommended as the default quantization starting point as typically close to lossless for inference with more headroom than INT8 or INT4, with escalation to quantization-aware training only when post-training loss exceeds acceptable thresholds.
insights.speaker: Prerana Gambhir
insights.so_what: FP8 as the enterprise default favors hardware with native FP8 support, an architectural moat for newer accelerator generations over older FP16-era fleets.
insights.quote: FP8 is the recommended starting point – typically close to lossless for inference, with more headroom than INT8 or INT4.

insights.claim: Freed memory from quantization can be spent two ways — moving to a smaller GPU, or fitting a larger batch or longer KV cache on the same GPU to raise throughput and lower cost per token.
insights.speaker: Prerana Gambhir
insights.so_what: The second path means efficiency gains can be absorbed as more tokens served rather than fewer GPUs bought — the Jevons-style dynamic that keeps hardware demand intact despite optimization.
insights.quote: That freed memory lets you drop to a smaller GPU, or fit a larger batch or longer KV cache on the same GPU to raise throughput and lower cost per token.

insights.claim: Post-training quantization needs only a small set of representative prompts for a calibration pass that sets per-layer scaling factors, and is shown as a few lines of ModelOpt code applied to an already-trained checkpoint.
insights.speaker: Prerana Gambhir
insights.so_what: Near-zero adoption friction means quantization diffuses fast across the installed base — assume most production inference is already or soon 8-bit when modeling effective serving capacity.
insights.quote: It’s the “quick win” because it needs no retraining.

themes.theme: Pruning and distillation for deeper compression

insights.claim: Depth pruning a Qwen3-8B teacher from 36 to 24 layers and width pruning ffn_hidden_size from 12288 to 9216 and hidden_size from 4096 to 3584 both land at roughly 6B parameters, after which distillation against the original teacher recovers accuracy.
insights.speaker: Prerana Gambhir
insights.so_what: Two structurally different routes to the same parameter budget means model compression is now a tunable engineering dial, letting enterprises target a specific GPU tier rather than accept vendor-released model sizes.
insights.quote: depth pruning trims 36->24 layers, while width pruning shrinks ffn_hidden_size 12288->9216 and hidden_size 4096->3584, both yielding roughly 6B parameters

insights.claim: In the demonstrated run, width pruning reached a lower final validation loss (3.21 vs 3.60) while depth pruning converged faster, an explicit quality-versus-training-time tradeoff between the two compression routes.
insights.speaker: Prerana Gambhir
insights.so_what: The authors flag the dataset as small and the numbers illustrative, so treat the ranking as directional; the actionable point is that the tradeoff exists and must be tested per workload.
insights.quote: in this run width pruning reached a lower final validation loss (3.21 vs 3.60), while depth pruning converged faster
insights.locator: Figure 2. Pruning validation loss: Depth vs. width

insights.claim: An NVIDIA published run produced a 6B depth-pruned model that is 30% faster than Qwen3-4B while scoring higher on MMLU (72.5 versus 70.0), meaning a compressed larger model beat a natively smaller one on both speed and accuracy.
insights.speaker: Prerana Gambhir
insights.so_what: Compressing down from a strong teacher can dominate training a small model from scratch — this favors organizations with access to large open checkpoints and undercuts the value of small-model-only labs.
insights.quote: the NVIDIA published run produces a 6B depth-pruned model that is 30% faster than Qwen3-4B at higher MMLU accuracy (72.5 vs 70.0)

insights.claim: The pruning workflow requires only 2x NVIDIA H100 or A100 80GB GPUs with the NeMo container, and pruning itself runs single-GPU because FastNAS asserts tp_size=1 for both depth and width pruning.
insights.speaker: Prerana Gambhir
insights.so_what: A two-GPU entry point puts model compression within reach of mid-size enterprises, not just labs — widening the population able to run custom models on cheap inference hardware.
insights.quote: Prerequisites: 2x NVIDIA H100 or A100 80GB GPUs, a Docker-enabled environment, and the NeMo container

insights.claim: The one-time compute cost of pruning and distillation is framed as offset by sustained savings in hardware utilization, power, and operational overhead at enterprise scale.
insights.speaker: Prerana Gambhir
insights.so_what: Power is named alongside hardware as a recurring saving, reinforcing that datacenter energy cost is now a first-order input in AI deployment economics.
insights.quote: At enterprise scale, the cumulative savings in hardware, power, and operational overhead justify the investment.
insights.locator: Optimizing models for a better TCO

insights.claim: GPU sizing is presented as an ongoing optimization loop rather than a fixed decision made at deployment, with quantization, pruning, and distillation to be revisited as models and workloads evolve.
insights.speaker: Prerana Gambhir
insights.so_what: Continuous re-optimization implies enterprise GPU footprints get repeatedly re-benchmarked, creating churn risk for locked-in multi-year capacity contracts.
insights.quote: GPU sizing is an ongoing optimization, not a fixed choice made at deployment.

insights.claim: The stated endpoint of the optimization sequence is smaller, faster models that expand AI's reach across mobile, edge, and embedded applications — an explicit push of inference beyond the datacenter.
insights.speaker: Prerana Gambhir
insights.so_what: Watch for edge/embedded inference silicon as the next demand leg once compression makes capable models fit; this is where compressed-model economics create new markets rather than shrinking existing ones.
insights.quote: producing smaller, faster models that expand AI’s reach across mobile, edge, and embedded applications

insights.claim: NVIDIA is publishing a detailed playbook for buying fewer and smaller GPUs, positioning its ModelOpt and NeMo software as the tooling layer through which that optimization happens.
insights.speaker: Prerana Gambhir
insights.so_what: The vendor is trading per-unit hardware demand for lock-in at the software and toolchain layer, betting that cheaper inference expands total token volume — a strategic tell worth weighing against pure hardware-cycle theses.
insights.locator: Optimizing models for a better TCO
